title: Diwali Airfare Surge: Delhi–Bengaluru Tickets Cross ₹20,000 as Festival Rush Squeezes Seats
excerpt: A viral post spotlighting a ₹13,000-to-₹20,000+ jump on the Delhi–Bengaluru route has become the face of this year's festive fare surge, as tighter seat capacity, costlier jet fuel and dynamic pricing collide ahead of the November 8 festival.
body:
• A viral post showing Delhi–Bengaluru Diwali fares jumping from roughly ₹13,000 to over ₹20,000 has become this festive season’s most-shared travel grievance, reported by News18.
  • Travel portals show return fares for the Diwali window climbing sharply: up to ₹18,000 on Delhi–Hyderabad, ₹16,000 on Delhi–Bengaluru and ₹13,000 on Delhi–Mumbai.
  • Aviation data firm OAG says Indian domestic seat capacity fell about 5.6% in September, while aviation turbine fuel prices rose for a second consecutive month — supply is tightest just as demand peaks.
  • The DGCA has asked carriers to add capacity and keep fares reasonable; IndiGo, Air India and SpiceJet together will operate more than 1,700 extra flights through October and November.

A screenshot of a flight-booking page has become the symbol of this year’s Diwali travel scramble. A traveller who searched for tickets between Delhi and Bengaluru for the festival week found fares that had jumped from roughly ₹13,000 to more than ₹20,000 — and posted the comparison with a blunt question: what happened to flight prices? The post went viral, and News18 picked up the story, triggering a wave of similar complaints from passengers across the country.

The anger is easy to understand. Diwali — the main festival night falls on Sunday, November 8 this year, with the five-day celebration running from November 6 to 10 — is the biggest homecoming season in the Indian calendar. For the lakhs of professionals, students and migrant workers who live far from their families, the festival means a flight home.

The numbers behind the surge

"For the lakhs of professionals, students and migrant workers who live far from their families, the festival means a flight home."

Fare-tracking across major routes paints a consistent picture. Return fares for the Diwali period are running far above off-season levels: up to ₹18,000 on Delhi–Hyderabad with Air India, up to ₹17,000 on Delhi–Kolkata, up to ₹16,000 on Delhi–Bengaluru and up to ₹13,000 on Delhi–Mumbai with IndiGo, according to a survey of travel portals.

Three forces are converging. First, demand is unusually concentrated: thousands of workers stream out of Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi, Hyderabad and Chennai for their home cities within a narrow window, and the cheapest fare buckets sell out first under airlines’ dynamic pricing models. Second, capacity has shrunk — aviation data agency OAG reports that domestic seat capacity fell by about 5.6% in September, with IndiGo cutting roughly 4.5% and Air India about 8.8%, as fleet-delivery delays, engine-maintenance backlogs and operational adjustments take aircraft out of service. With the two carriers controlling more than 90% of the domestic market, the shortfall is felt everywhere. Third, fuel costs are climbing: aviation turbine fuel prices rose 5.46%, or ₹6.28 per litre, to ₹121.28 per litre on September 1 — the second consecutive monthly increase. Fuel accounts for roughly 35–40% of an airline’s operating costs.

Regulator steps in, airlines add flights

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation has intervened. With the festive season approaching, the regulator instructed airlines to expand capacity and keep ticket prices reasonable after reviewing fare patterns on major domestic routes. Following the advisory, IndiGo — which holds about 64% of the domestic market — said it would add around 730 flights across 42 routes, Air India and Air India Express together will deploy nearly 486 flights on 20 sectors, and SpiceJet is introducing about 546 flights across 38 routes. Airlines are free to set their own fares under India’s open-skies policy, but the government retains the authority to step in when prices rise excessively, and the DGCA said it would closely monitor fares and availability during the rush.

What travellers can do

Travel analysts say the pattern is predictable enough to plan around. Fares are lowest for those who book 60 to 90 days in advance, and flying on the day of the festival itself — when most people want to have already arrived — is consistently cheaper than flying in the days before. Checking alternate nearby airports and staying flexible by even a day or two around the peak window can also shave thousands off a ticket.

A note for NRIs planning the trip home

The surge matters beyond domestic travellers. NRIs who combine an international trip with domestic legs — or who book tickets for family members flying in from other Indian cities — face the same dynamic pricing. With Diwali falling on a Sunday this year, the long weekend around November 8 is shaping up to be one of the most expensive windows to fly, so locking in domestic connections early, alongside international segments, is the simplest hedge.

What’s next

If history is any guide, fares will keep climbing as departure dates approach and the cheapest buckets empty out. The real test of the DGCA’s intervention will be whether the 1,700-plus additional flights are enough to take the edge off prices on the most in-demand routes. With Chhath Puja following close behind Diwali, the pressure on fares is unlikely to ease before mid-November.
image_caption: An Air India aircraft in flight during peak festive-season travel. Delhi-Bengaluru fares for Diwali have surged past Rs 20,000, up from around Rs 13,000, prompting complaints from travellers about festive pricing.
nri_angle: NRIs combining international trips with domestic legs — or booking family members' festive-season travel within India — face the same Diwali fare surge, making early booking of domestic connections the simplest hedge.
